title: Reversal in HIV testing uptake among adolescent girls in Zambia, 2007–2024: A decomposition analysis of four Demographic and Health Surveys
content:
by Samson Shumba, Maureen Aongola, Deborah Tembo

Background

Zambia expanded HIV testing substantially during the 2010s, but testing strategies changed after 2018 with the shift to targeted testing and the COVID-19 pandemic. We examined trends in HIV testing among adolescent girls between 2007 and 2024, and whether changes reflected shifts in the characteristics of adolescent girls or in how those characteristics related to testing.

Methods

We pooled data on 11,717 girls aged 15–19 years from the 2007, 2013/14, 2018 and 2024 Zambia Demographic and Health Surveys. Outcomes were ever having been tested for HIV and having been tested in the past 12 months and received the result. We used survey-weighted logistic regression, interaction models to estimate subgroup-specific changes, and multivariate decomposition, with Fairlie decomposition as a sensitivity analysis, to separate compositional change from changes in effects.

Results

Ever-testing rose from 23.0% in 2007 to 60.9% in 2018, then fell to 49.3% in 2024 (adjusted change −11.4 percentage points, 95% CI −14.0 to −8.8). Recent testing fell from 47.4% to 31.2% over the same period. Among girls who had ever been pregnant, ever-testing did not change (+2.7 percentage points, 95% CI −1.0 to 6.4), whereas among those who had never been pregnant it fell by 16.9 points (95% CI −20.3 to −13.4). Declines were also larger among urban than rural girls (−15.6 vs −6.9 points) and in wealthier quintiles. Ever having been pregnant was the strongest factor associated with testing (AOR 9.79, 95% CI 8.15–11.76). Changes in population characteristics explained less than 5% of the decline in all specifications, and about 6% of the earlier rise. Self-test use was about 2% in both 2018 and 2024.

Conclusions

HIV testing among adolescent girls in Zambia reversed after 2018. The decline occurred almost entirely outside the antenatal pathway and was not explained by changes in the population. Restoring adolescent testing will require entry points beyond antenatal care and monitoring of adolescent testing coverage alongside positivity yield.
